intro: The Torah ends with Moses looking at the land from a mountain. This unit begins on the other side of the river. The books of Joshua and Judges tell how the people came into the land and how they lived there, tribe by tribe, with no king. Leaders called judges stepped up when trouble came. Some were wise, like Deborah. Some were brave, like Gideon. Some were strong but made big mistakes, like Samson.

Then the unit turns to two families. In the book of Ruth, a young woman from Moab chooses to stay with her mother-in-law. In the first book of Samuel, a woman named Hannah prays for a son. That son, Samuel, grows up to hear a voice in the night and to lead the people. At the end, the people ask him for a king.

In this unit you will learn where these books sit in the Tanakh, what they say, and how Jewish readers have read them. You will meet a Hebrew word, chesed, that means loyal kindness. And you will practice saying "the text says" and "Jewish tradition teaches" when you tell what you found.
bigQuestion: What do the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth and 1 Samuel say about courage, loyalty and the kind of leader a people needs?

timeline.t: Joshua becomes leader after Moses and is told to be strong and brave
The people march around Jericho for seven days, and the wall falls
Joshua gathers the tribes at Shechem and asks them to choose to serve God
Deborah judges under a palm tree and goes to battle with Barak
Gideon's army shrinks to three hundred men
Samson tells Delilah his secret and loses his strength
The book ends: in those days there was no king in Israel
Ruth promises Naomi: where you go, I will go
Boaz redeems the family; Ruth's great-grandson will be David
Hannah prays at Shiloh and Samuel is born
Samuel hears a voice in the night and answers, speak, I am listening
The elders ask Samuel for a king like other nations

words.d: the Prophets, the second part of the Tanakh; Joshua is its first book
in the book of Judges, a leader who stepped up in a crisis; not a king
a ram's horn blown like a trumpet; seven were blown at Jericho
a large family group; the book of Joshua divides the land among twelve
a woman the text says spoke for God, like Deborah
a person set apart by promises such as not cutting hair; Samson was one
a reading from the Prophets read in synagogue after the Torah portion
to gather grain the harvesters left; the Torah keeps it for the poor and the stranger
a redeemer; a close relative who helps a family that has lost its land or its men
the holiday seven weeks after Passover, when the book of Ruth is read
to pour oil on someone's head as a sign they are chosen to lead
loyal kindness; kindness that keeps a promise even when it costs something

test.q: Which book is the first in Nevi'im, the Prophets?
test.why: The Tanakh's second part, Nevi'im, begins with the book of Joshua, right after the Torah.

test.q: Who hid the two spies on her roof in Jericho?
test.why: Joshua 2 says Rahab of Jericho hid the spies and was kept safe when the city fell.

test.q: What does the book of Joshua say the people did at Jericho for six days?
choices: Marched around the city once a day
test.why: Joshua 6 says the people marched around Jericho once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh.

test.q: Which tribe got towns spread across the land instead of one big share?
test.why: The book of Joshua says the Levites, who helped with worship, got towns in every tribe's land.

test.q: In the book of Judges, what did a judge do?
choices: Ruled as king from a palace
Stepped up to lead in a crisis
test.why: The judges were rescuers and leaders in a crisis; the book says there was no king in those days.

test.q: Who went to battle only after Deborah agreed to go too?
test.why: Judges 4:8 says Barak would go only if Deborah went with him.

test.q: How many men did Gideon keep after the test at the stream?
test.why: Judges 7 says only three hundred lapped water from their hands, and Gideon kept them.

test.q: Which people did Samson fight, according to the book of Judges?
test.why: Samson's enemies in Judges 13–16 are the Philistines, who lived by the sea.

test.q: What is the last line of the book of Judges about?
choices: There was no king, and everyone did what seemed right to them
test.why: Judges 21:25 says there was no king in Israel and every person did what was right in their own eyes.

test.q: What did Ruth say to Naomi on the road?
choices: I will go back to Moab
Where you go, I will go
test.why: Ruth 1:16 says: whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people.

test.q: In which part of the Tanakh is the book of Ruth found?
test.why: Ruth is one of the five Megillot in Ketuvim, the Writings, and is read on Shavuot.

test.q: What was Ruth doing in Boaz's field?
test.why: Ruth 2 says Ruth gleaned, gathering grain the harvesters left, as the Torah allows for the poor.

test.q: What did Hannah promise about her son?
choices: He would serve God all his life
test.why: 1 Samuel 1:11 says Hannah promised to give her son to serve God, and she brought Samuel to Shiloh.

test.q: What did Samuel say when the voice called him the fourth time?
choices: Where you go, I will go
Speak, for your servant is listening
test.why: 1 Samuel 3:10 says Samuel answered as Eli taught him: speak, for Thy servant heareth.

test.q: What did Samuel warn a king would take from the people?
choices: Their sons, daughters, fields and crops
test.why: In 1 Samuel 8, Samuel lists what a king takes: sons, daughters, the best fields and a tenth of the crops.

write.prompt: What kind of leader do these books say a people needs? Pick two people from the unit, like Deborah (Judges 4), Gideon (Judges 7), Ruth (Ruth 1) or Samuel (1 Samuel 3 or 8). For each, tell what the text says they did and what Jewish readers have seen in it. Then say what the two stories have in common.
tips: Name the book and chapter each time you tell part of a story, like "Judges 7 says."
Say "the text says" for what happens and "Jewish tradition teaches" for what readers have taken from it.
Use two words from the unit, like judge, chesed, haftarah or anoint.
Compare the two people. Do not say one is good and one is bad; say what each one did.
Keep your sentences short. One idea in each sentence.
